Anugoonj Engage: Nineteen Capabilities

A customer-engagement platform, a margin covenant, and a usage table that cannot see a third of the revenue.

1. Bandra, Sunday night, 8 March 2026

Kabir Deshmukh had two documents open and could not reconcile them.

It was a little past eleven on the Sunday of the long Holi weekend, and from the balcony of his flat in Bandra West he could still hear music from the building opposite. On the laptop in front of him were two spreadsheets. The first, prepared by the product analytics team in Bengaluru, ranked all nineteen of Anugoonj Engage's capabilities by the share of customer accounts that had used each of them in the quarter to February 2026. The second, prepared by customer success in Singapore, ranked the same nineteen capabilities by the share of accounts recorded as "actively deployed" in the quarterly business review template. For six of the nineteen, the two documents disagreed by more than twenty percentage points. For one of them — Predictive Journeys, the capability Anugoonj had paid ₹74 crore to acquire in 2023 — they disagreed by thirty-two.

At nine the next morning Kabir was due to present a consolidation plan to Ananya Pillai, Anugoonj's co-founder and chief executive, and to the two directors who sat on the operating committee. The plan was supposed to name the capabilities that would be sunset over the next three quarters, the engineering capacity that would be released, and the gross-margin improvement that would follow. The margin number was not a matter of preference. Anugoonj had drawn ₹120 crore of venture debt in November, and the facility carried a covenant: gross margin of at least 68 per cent by the quarter ending December 2026. The company had closed February at 61.4 per cent.

Kabir had been chief product officer for two years and had built his reputation on evidence. He had spent the weekend trying to work out which of his two spreadsheets was the evidence.

2. How Anugoonj got here, and the decision that still binds

Anugoonj Engage was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by Ananya Pillai and Vivek Raghavan, who had met building notification infrastructure at a large Indian e-commerce firm. The product began as a single thing: a reliable way for consumer companies to send transactional and promotional messages across SMS, email and push, with retry logic that worked on Indian telecom networks. By March 2026 it served 410 enterprise customers, employed 640 people across Bengaluru, Pune, Mumbai, Singapore, Berlin, Toronto and New Jersey, and carried ₹218 crore of annual recurring revenue.

The decision that constrained everything Kabir could now do had been taken in 2021. A large non-banking financial company — at the time Anugoonj's biggest prospective account, worth ₹9 crore a year — had refused to run customer data in a multi-tenant cloud. Vivek had argued that refusing the deal would be the disciplined choice. Ananya had taken the deal, and Anugoonj had built a separately deployable edition, internally called Core-X, that ran inside the customer's own virtual private cloud.

Core-X won the NBFC, and then it won eleven more regulated accounts. By February 2026 it carried ₹68 crore of ARR — 31 per cent of the company's revenue — across fourteen accounts, most of them banks, insurers and one state-owned utility. It also ran on a codebase that had diverged from the cloud edition over five years. Every capability Anugoonj shipped had to be built once and then ported, usually at between 40 and 70 per cent of the original cost. And Core-X emitted no product telemetry to Anugoonj at all. Customers had insisted on it in 2021, the contracts said so, and nobody had revisited the clause.

The second consequential decision was the 2023 acquisition of Tarkash AI, a fourteen-person Pune company with a propensity-modelling engine, for ₹74 crore in cash and stock. Tarkash's technology became Predictive Journeys: a capability that chose, per customer, which message to send and when. It had been the centre of Anugoonj's positioning ever since. Ananya had described it to the board in October 2025 as "the reason we are not a messaging pipe."

3. The industry around it

Anugoonj sold into a crowded and capable Indian market. MoEngage, CleverTap, Netcore and WebEngage all competed for the same enterprise marketing budgets, and international platforms sat above them in the largest accounts. Differentiation had become difficult to sustain; most vendors had shipped comparable journey builders, comparable segmentation and, since 2024, comparable generative-AI content assistants.

Three external forces bore directly on the March decision. The first was channel economics. WhatsApp had become the dominant engagement channel for Indian consumer brands, and Meta's move to per-message pricing by category had changed the arithmetic for every platform that resold it: volume had risen sharply while the margin on each message had compressed, because a growing share of Anugoonj's revenue was pass-through. SMS volumes, which carried better margins for Anugoonj under its aggregator contracts, had been falling for three years, and TRAI's DLT registration regime made SMS operationally heavier for customers in any case.

The second was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Consent management had moved from a checkbox to an architecture, and Anugoonj's regulated customers — and the RBI-supervised ones especially — had begun asking for consent artefacts, purpose limitation and retention controls that the cloud edition supported and Core-X supported differently.

The third was exposure outside India. Anugoonj's largest single account was Dareen Retail Group in Dubai — ₹14.6 crore a year across grocery, fashion and pharmacy banners in the UAE, Oman and Saudi Arabia. Dareen's contract, signed in 2024 and renewing in October 2026, contained a clause requiring ninety days' written notice before the withdrawal of any capability in use, and an Arabic-language requirement that only two of Anugoonj's nineteen capabilities fully met.

4. The situation, in sequence

In August 2025, with growth slowing from 34 per cent to 19 per cent year on year, the board asked for a path to profitability by FY28. Ananya proposed, and the board accepted, a plan built on two levers: raising average revenue per account through Predictive Journeys attach, and reducing cost of revenue by consolidating infrastructure. It was believed at the time that Predictive Journeys was attached to roughly 40 per cent of accounts and could reach 70 per cent.

In November 2025, Anugoonj drew the ₹120 crore debt facility to fund the consolidation without further dilution. The 68 per cent margin covenant was agreed in the same week. It was believed that the compute cost of Predictive Journeys was around ₹4 crore a year.

In December 2025, Kabir asked the analytics team for a full capability audit. Meera Krishnan, the head of product analytics in Bengaluru, delivered the first cut in January. It showed Predictive Journeys running in 12 per cent of accounts by telemetry — not 40 — and it showed that eight of the nineteen capabilities were used by fewer than 15 per cent of accounts.

In late January 2026, Wei Jian Ong in Singapore disputed the audit. His QBR records showed Predictive Journeys "actively deployed" in 44 per cent of accounts. The discrepancy was traced, partly. Core-X accounts, which included four of the five largest, emitted no telemetry at all; Meera's denominator therefore included them while her numerator could not. When Core-X accounts were removed from both, Predictive Journeys reached 17 per cent by telemetry. The gap to 44 per cent remained unexplained.

In February 2026, the finance team re-costed compute by capability for the first time. Predictive Journeys had consumed ₹11.3 crore in the preceding twelve months, not ₹4 crore. The model retrained nightly per account regardless of whether the account had sent a campaign that month. Twenty-nine accounts had it enabled and had not sent a predictive campaign since June 2025; they had been retraining every night since.

On 3 March, Dr Ishita Nair, the principal data scientist in Toronto who had led the Tarkash integration, sent Kabir a note observing that the accounts using Predictive Journeys had 23 per cent higher net revenue retention than those that did not — and adding, in the same paragraph, that she could not separate this from the fact that Anugoonj's customer-success team preferentially enabled the capability for its healthiest accounts. Ishita's parental leave began on 20 March.

5. The people

Ananya Pillai, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: the company must consolidate to hit the covenant, and it must do so without conceding that Anugoonj is a messaging utility. Incentive: she has told the board twice that Predictive Journeys is the strategic core, and the ₹74 crore acquisition was hers. Not saying: she has had two exploratory conversations about a strategic investment that would value Anugoonj on an AI multiple rather than a messaging multiple.

Vivek Raghavan, co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru. Position: Core-X must be sunset; it is the single largest drag on velocity and margin, and everything else is a distraction. Incentive: he opposed the 2021 decision and has been proved partly right. Not saying: his own platform team's re-architecture programme is four months behind, and consolidating onto the cloud edition would put that delay on the critical path.

Shalini Bose, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: Core-X accounts are the most profitable in the company at the gross level and should be defended; the fork is manageable with better tooling. Incentive: her Pune organisation of 71 engineers exists substantially to maintain and extend Core-X. Not saying: two of her senior engineers have resigned in the last month and she has not yet backfilled them.

Wei Jian Ong, VP Customer Success, Singapore. Position: the telemetry audit is unreliable and the QBR record is the ground truth, because his team sits with customers. Incentive: his team's quarterly scorecard includes a "product depth" measure — capabilities deployed per account — which feeds into variable pay. Not saying: the QBR field is filled in by the account manager at the start of the quarter and is rarely corrected.

Gautam Sethi, SVP Sales, New Jersey. Position: nothing should be removed before the FY27 selling season; feature parity is what gets Anugoonj shortlisted against larger competitors. Incentive: compensated on new bookings, with an accelerator on multi-capability deals. Not saying: three of his five largest 2025 wins were priced on messaging volume alone and the additional capabilities were given away.

Lukas Brenner, Head of Design, Berlin. Position: the product has nineteen capabilities and one navigation, and the adoption problem for at least five of them is that nobody can find them; removing them would be measuring the wrong thing. Incentive: he has been asking for a navigation redesign for three quarters. Not saying: his own research sample was twenty-two users, nineteen of them in India, and none from a Core-X account.

Meera Krishnan, Head of Product Analytics, Bengaluru. Position: the telemetry is what it is, and the honest presentation is to report the 69 per cent of revenue she can see and to mark the rest as unknown. Incentive: professional credibility rests on the audit she delivered. Not saying: three of the nineteen capabilities were instrumented only in October 2025, so their twelve-month figures are extrapolations she made herself.

Ishita Nair, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: the retention correlation around Predictive Journeys is real but probably not causal, and a holdout would settle it in eight weeks. Incentive: she built the integration and would prefer it not be dismantled. Not saying: she believes the nightly retraining schedule is indefensible and has said so only to Kabir.

8. The options as Kabir sees them

By Sunday night Kabir had written three options on a page, and had begun to suspect that the page itself was the problem.

Option A — sunset the tail. Withdraw six capabilities over three quarters: survey and feedback, custom dashboards, web personalisation, multilingual content, offline event ingest, and the generative content assistant, retaining Predictive Journeys. This releases roughly 33 engineering FTE and ₹15.9 crore of compute and port cost, which finance believes is worth between four and five margin points. It also removes the two capabilities Faisal named as daily-use at Dareen, and multilingual content sits on ₹27.2 crore of ARR concentrated in accounts serving non-English markets.

Option B — sunset the centre. Withdraw or radically reduce Predictive Journeys: stop nightly retraining, move it to an on-demand paid add-on at ₹18 lakh a year, and let adoption reveal willingness to pay. This releases ₹11.3 crore of compute and 14 FTE immediately and tests the causal question Ishita cannot answer. It also contradicts three years of positioning, reverses Ananya's acquisition, and would have to be explained to the board in the same quarter as the margin covenant.

Option C — end the fork instead. Keep all nineteen capabilities and consolidate Core-X onto the cloud edition over eighteen months, which Vivek argues frees more capacity than any capability decision could. This requires fourteen regulated customers carrying ₹68 crore — at the highest gross margin in the company — to accept a deployment change, and Shalini's estimate of the migration cost differs from Vivek's by a factor she has not been asked to reconcile.

What unsettled Kabir was a fourth thought he had not written down. Exhibit 3 said that the margin problem was principally a channel-mix problem: WhatsApp at 38 per cent margin rising toward 60 per cent of volume. If that was the dominant term, then every capability on his list could be removed and the covenant would still be missed. The nineteen-capability question might be the one he could answer rather than the one that mattered — and Monday's meeting had been convened to answer it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The operating committee met at nine on Monday 9 March. The board met on 27 March, and the debt facility required a quarterly covenant certificate.

The constraints were these. Gross margin must reach 68 per cent by the quarter ending December 2026; February closed at 61.4 per cent. Headcount was frozen at 640 until September; any capacity had to come from reallocation. The Dareen contract required ninety days' written notice for the withdrawal of any capability in use, which put the last safe date for a Dareen-affecting announcement at early July if the October renewal was not to be disturbed. Four Core-X contracts contained a clause obliging Anugoonj to maintain the in-VPC deployment through their current terms, the longest running to March 2028. DPDP consent obligations applied regardless of any product decision and consumed an estimated six FTE for the year. Ishita Nair's leave began on 20 March, and no holdout design had been written. And three of the nineteen capabilities had been sold, with delivery commitments, into deals Gautam had closed in the December quarter.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibits 1 and 2 report on the same nineteen capabilities and disagree. Reconstruct, as far as the case allows, what each exhibit actually measures, on what base, and produced by whom for what purpose. Which differences are explained, and which are not?

2. Exhibit 1 ranks capabilities by breadth. What alternative denominators could be defended for offline event ingest, multilingual content and Predictive Journeys, and how far does each re-basing change the ranking?

3. Exhibit 5 shows six stages. Where is Predictive Journeys' population genuinely lost, and what does the default-on policy do to the interpretation of each bar? What would you need to observe to tell an onboarding problem from a value problem here?

4. Ishita reports 23 per cent higher net revenue retention among Predictive Journeys accounts and says she cannot separate it from selection. Design the cheapest study that would settle the question, and state what it would cost in revenue, time and political capital — and whether it can be run before 20 March.

5. Vivek and Shalini disagree about whether the fork or the channel mix is the margin problem, and Exhibit 3 is not in the same pack as Exhibits 1, 2 and 4. What would you have to believe for each of them to be right, and what evidence in the case bears on it?

6. What should Kabir do on Monday morning — what does he present, what does he refuse to present, and what does he ask for? And when the board meets on 27 March, what should he tell it about the nineteen capabilities, the covenant, and the thirty-one per cent of revenue he cannot see?

11. Bandra, a little after one

The music across the road had stopped. Kabir had closed both spreadsheets and opened a third document, empty, titled Monday.

He kept returning to a sentence in Meera's covering note: I would rather publish "unknown" than publish a number that will be quoted for a year. It was the right instinct and it was also, he thought, unaffordable. The committee would not adjourn because the instrument was imperfect. Somebody would present a ranking on Monday, and if it was not his it would be Wei Jian's, or Gautam's, or the one finance had already built from Exhibit 4 without telling him.

He thought about Faisal in Dubai, who could not name a single person using the capability Anugoonj had spent ₹74 crore to acquire, and who would notice within a week if Arabic templates stopped working. He thought about Shalini's seventy-one engineers in Pune and the two resignations she had mentioned only in passing. He thought about the covenant, and about Exhibit 3, and about the possibility that the meeting he had spent three months preparing for was a meeting about the wrong question.

The document stayed empty. Outside, the first crows had started, which meant it was nearer to morning than he had allowed.
